name: PT Austindo Nusantara Jaya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Austindo Nusantara Jaya: a First Resources estate the float cannot arbitrage
frontmatter.summary: A 40,136 ha palm estate controlled 91.2% by First Resources, selling 94.6% of revenue to group companies on formula prices with a 1.6% free float. The filing-restated DCF says NAV is far above the price; we stay BUY with a liquidity warning and a valuation the minority cannot force.
thesis: Pure palm again: the West Papua estates were sold and the sago/edamame units discontinued, so the FY2025 loss is a divestment charge, not an operating loss - operating profit was IDR816.1bn [S3].
Through-cycle CPO value: the DCF on the house d.agri.cpo deck, calibrated to the FY2025 realised price, gives Rp3,934 a share; the EV/EBITDA and P/BV cross-checks sit far below and we say why.
The controlling shareholder is the business model: 94.6% of 9M 2026 revenue goes to First Resources companies, and IDR1,124.0bn was lent to an affiliate while IDR1,390.0bn was borrowed [S4].
The float, not the value, is binding: a 1.6% free float and thin turnover justify the 20% discount that takes the weighted value to Rp2,768 [S0].
No dividend anchor yet: nil for three years and a modest payout assumption that is a judgment, not a policy [S3].

catalysts.event: Monthly export levy and duty reset after the November cut - if the lower charge holds, realised prices rise
DSI publishes the formal service fee for the single-window palm export platform
DSI platform goes live for all palm and derivative shipments - first test of administrative delay
FY2026 audited results - first clean year under First Resources and the first test of the payout

blocks.text: We stay at **BUY** with a target of **Rp2,768**, 107.1% above the Rp1,365 price: 60% through-cycle DCF at Rp3,934, 25% EV/EBITDA at Rp2,448 and 15% P/BV at Rp1,589, rolled forward at the cost of equity and cut by the 20% liquidity discount for a 1.6% float [S0, S3]. The discount takes the weighted value from Rp3,460 to Rp2,768; the risk section explains why a float this thin earns it.

Two things changed in this revision. The EV/EBITDA leg is back at its industry weight, with trailing EBITDA rebuilt from the annual report's line names rather than the pack's understated cash-flow figure [S3, F58, F59, S0, S4]. Long-run volume is capped at the area and yield ceiling the filing supports, 332.0 kt, and each scenario carries four shocks including an explicit cost‑per‑tonne flex for CPO‑linked bought‑in FFB and resale purchases [S3, F7, F19, F26, F9, F24].

The company changed shape in 2025: First Resources became controlling shareholder with 91.2%, the West Papua subsidiaries were divested and sago and edamame discontinued [S2, S3]. What remains is a single-segment palm producer - 40,136 ha planted, 33,288 ha mature, 254 kt of CPO in FY2025 [S3, F7, F19, F5]. The FY2025 loss is a divestment charge, not an operating loss: operating profit was IDR816.1bn against a divestment loss of -72.1 USD m, and the nine-month 2026 operating profit of IDR1,059.0bn shows the cleaned-up business [S3, S4, F20].

The variant view is not the CPO price, which the house deck already sets; it is whether a minority can capture the value. 94.6% of 9M 2026 revenue was sold to First Resources group companies under formula pricing, and the company lent IDR1,124.0bn to one of them at eight and a half per cent while borrowing IDR1,390.0bn long term [S4, F16, F17, F23]. The estate is worth far more than the market pays, nothing in the next twelve months forces the gap closed, and the stock is a value holding with a governance and liquidity tax rather than a catalyst-driven trade.

Indonesian palm companies are valued on a through-cycle CPO price and an enterprise value per planted hectare, because a mature estate is a long-lived annuity whose earnings swing with one commodity. When a strategic owner holds almost all the shares, the market price can sit below fundamental value for years because there is no float to arbitrage the gap.

ANJT is an upstream palm producer: it grows fresh fruit bunches, buys fruit from third parties and plasma cooperatives, and mills it into crude palm oil and palm kernel. In FY2025 own FFB was 768 kt and third-party purchases 472 kt, so close to two-fifths of the 1,234 kt milled was bought in; CPO production was 254 kt at an extraction rate of 20.6% [S3, F5, F8, F9, F25, F26].

The footprint sits in Belitung (PT Sahabat Mewah dan Makmur, 17,360 ha), West Kalimantan at Ketapang, North Sumatra at Siais (PT Austindo Nusantara Jaya Agri Siais, 9,412 ha) and South Sumatra [S3, F36, F37]. Of the 40,136 ha planted, 33,288 ha is mature and 6,848 ha is immature, about a fifth of the mature area [S3, F7, F19, F49]. The immature hectares add roughly a tenth to output once bearing - palm takes three to four years to first harvest - so the 2024-2025 plantings come on stream from FY2028E and take long-run volume to 332.0 kt; the 1,472 ha replanted in 2025 holds mature area flat and no new planting or mill is announced: a maturing asset, not a growth programme [S3, F8, F19, F26, F28, F49].

Because close to two-fifths of mill intake is bought in, the margin depends on the CPO-to-FFB spread [S3, S4]. In 2026 the company also began buying finished palm products for resale - IDR717.9bn in the nine months - which lifted revenue and cost of revenue without changing the estate; small against the asset but large against profit, it makes reported revenue growth overstate operating growth in FY2026E [S4, F24].

Strategy under First Resources is consolidation, not expansion: replanting of 1,472 ha in 2025, mainly at ANJA and SMM, and no new planting or mill [S3, F28]. At 254 kt of CPO a year ANJT is a mid-cap challenger whose advantage is mill intake rather than land bank [S3]. Management's rationale for the acquisition was to secure feedstock for First Resources' downstream operations, which frames the estate as a supplier inside a group value chain - the source of the minority discount [S3].

Indonesian palm is a volume-and-price industry: the oil is a commodity, the buyer sets the reference, and the producer's durable lever is cost per tonne [S3, S6]. ANJT's economics are set by the CPO price, the export levy and duty wedge, the rupiah, and the share of mill intake bought in [S3, S4].

The house deck carries CPO at US$1,135/t for FY2026E and US$1,240/t for FY2027E against a FY2025 benchmark of US$1,007/t [deck: d.agri.cpo]. ANJT realised US$871/t a tonne in FY2025 and US$822/t in FY2024, below the benchmark in both years because the export charge and the group sales formula sit between the estate and the world price; the realisation ratio is calibrated on the last actual, not a forecast spike [S3, F3, F4].

The deck is not a spot forecast. The November 2026 government reference price of US$979/t is about an eighth below the FY2026E deck; the base case applies the FY2025-calibrated realisation of 86.5% to the through-cycle deck, whose FY2027E premium reflects the El Nino supply loss. The wedge is the export charge: in November 2026 the combined levy and duty fell a fifth to US$246/t a tonne, a sharper cut than the reference price, on a monthly-reset schedule [S6]. If the lower charge held, realisation would move toward nine-tenths; the schedule reverses as readily as it falls, so it is the bull case's realisation shock rather than a base-case input, with the bear case and sensitivity grid testing the gap [S5, S6, S7].

Supply is the swing factor: at its annual conference on 12 November 2026 GAPKI projected El Nino could cut the 2027 national crop by up to 3.0 Mt, above the 2.2 Mt reported at initiation [S5, S7]. The warning moved no model input: FY2027E volume stays at 300 kt because the projection names no region and ANJT's estates are in Sumatra, Belitung and Kalimantan, while the price side is already in the deck [S3, S7, deck: d.agri.cpo]; a proportional share of the national loss is the bear case's volume shock [S0].

From 1 January 2027 palm exports must pass through a single-window platform run by PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia; the interim fee is a single-digit US dollar amount, the formal tariff is due in December 2026, and the trading mechanism is unchanged [S8]. ANJT sells to group entities rather than exporting directly, so the fee lands first on the group channel: a few dollars a tonne plus a first-quarter delay risk, not a change to realisation [S4, S8].

Competitive position rests on cost: estate production cost of about Rp8.22m/t in 9M 2026 is flat to down on the year-ago period, and no peer cost curve is archived to rank it against [S4, F40, F51]. The estate keeps producing at a low margin in a trough, which is why a through-cycle DCF rather than a spot-earnings multiple is the primary method [S4, S6].

Five forces are set by the group channel: moderate supplier power, extreme buyer power with one group taking 94.6% of revenue, high entry barriers, slow substitution from soya and sunflower oil, and cost-based rivalry [S3, S4, F16, deck: d.agri.soyoil].

Revenue and volume. FY2025 revenue was IDR3,959.0bn on 270 kt of CPO-equivalent sales, with the kernel leg converted at each year's own realised ratio [S3, F1, F43, F44]. FY2026E models 300.0 kt from the nine-month actual, with revenue of IDR3,980.1bn a third above the year-ago period and including the new resale book [S4, F12, F24]. FY2027E is held at 300 kt because the GAPKI warning names no region; the proportional loss sits in the bear case [S5, S7]. From FY2028E volume follows the maturing estate - 305.0 kt, 315.0 kt, 322.0 kt and 328.0 kt - to a long-run 332.0 kt, the area and yield ceiling the filing supports, not a growth target [S3, F7, F19, F26, F28, F49].

Margins and costs. The estate: production cost of IDR2,090.8bn in 9M 2026 less D&A of IDR200.9bn is about Rp8.22m/t, against FY2025 cost of revenue of IDR2,562.0bn less restated D&A of IDR304.6bn [S3, S4, F10] - a stable base, not a squeezed one. The pass-through: IDR717.9bn of finished goods bought for resale at a near-zero spread [S4, F24]. Together they give the model's blended US$646.6 per tonne, held in real terms and escalated with rupiah inflation [S4, F13, F14]. The DSI fee is already netted inside the realisation ratio [S8, S4].

Earnings quality. Operating cash flow of IDR947.8bn in 9M 2026 covered net profit of IDR811.2bn, so reported profit is cash-backed [S4, F22, F29]. The composition of revenue is the flag: 94.6% is related-party, and a IDR1,124.0bn receivable from PT Adhitya Serayakorita sits in non-current assets at eight and a half per cent with no disclosed maturity [S4, F16, F17]. We carry it below face value in the bridge and treat recovery as a governance risk, and the FY2025 prior-period restatement is a disclosed optics-class flag, not a cash item [S3, S4].

Balance sheet. At 30 September 2026 cash was IDR1,149.1bn against short-term bank loans of IDR992.3bn, the long-term bank loan falling due within one year of IDR69.5bn and the long-term balance net of current maturities of IDR1,268.4bn, so net debt was IDR1,181.0bn, up from IDR723.0bn at the start of the year because the long-term facility funded the group loan [S4, F30, F31, F32, F62, F48]. Equity is IDR4,610.8bn and net debt is well under one year of FY2026E EBITDA [S4, F33]. The engine's pro-forma balance sheet rolls from the December 2025 pack, so the valuation uses the September bridge instead; and the interest line on opening debt at 8.8% understates FY2026E interest of IDR85.8bn after the drawdown, while FY2027E carries IDR205.1bn [S4].

Capex and working capital. 9M 2026 capex was IDR204.1bn and FY2025 capex IDR248.4bn, covering replanting and mill upkeep rather than expansion, and we hold capex near that run-rate [S3, F15]. Working capital is held at 16% of revenue; the observed ratio is inflated by the group receivable, a financing item, not a trading balance [S0, S4].

Capital allocation. No dividend for FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025; the last cash dividend relates to FY2022, and in 2026 the generated cash went to a IDR1,124.0bn related-party loan instead, funded by IDR1,390.0bn of new long-term debt [S3, S4, F17, F23]. We model a 20% payout from FY2026 because a 91.2% owner normally wants cash out, but that is a judgment, not policy: there is no fixed ratio, the AGM decides annually and the 2026 decision points the other way, so the target does not depend on the dividend [S3, S4]. The tax rate is 22%, in line with the effective charge [S4]. Terminal growth of 2.5% nominal is set from the deck's post-FY2029 path: the estate is planted out, capex roughly equals D&A, and the deck settles CPO at US$1,150/t long run while cash cost escalates with rupiah inflation [S3, deck: d.agri.cpo].

Why this method set. A palm estate is a long-lived, single-commodity cash-flow stream, so a through-cycle DCF is primary; multiples are cross-checks, because FY2026E is a mid-cycle year and capitalising mid-cycle EBITDA is the procyclical error the house method forbids [S4, deck: d.agri.cpo]. The weights are the industry default, restored because the filing cures the pack defect that had prompted dropping the EV/EBITDA leg. The engine capitalises trailing EBITDA, now built from the annual report's line names: FY2025 operating profit restated to IDR816.1bn, D&A to IDR304.6bn, rather than the pack's cash-flow-derived figure [S3, S4, F58, F10]. At 7.5 times that trailing EBITDA of IDR1,120.7bn less the net debt and minority bridge, the leg gives Rp2,448 a share, -37.8% against the DCF - a genuine cross-check below the DCF, not a floor above it [S0, S4]. FY2025 is the last audited year, so the leg does not lean on unaudited data. The September 2026 stub is stronger than a year earlier, so a true LTM figure would lift the leg - disclosed conservatism, not a correction [S4, F21, F60, F61].

The cost of capital is 11.3%: a 7.4% rupiah risk-free rate, a 4.2% mature-market equity risk premium, a 2.5% country risk premium, an unlevered beta of 0.80 levered to 1.12 at 0.51 debt/equity, a 13.3% cost of equity and a 9.4% pre-tax cost of debt [S0].

The rupiah rate is right because costs are rupiah and revenue is dollar-linked; the country premium captures export-charge policy risk, and we add no second governance premium beyond the liquidity discount [S0, S6]. The engine prices new debt at 9.4% while the interest line carries the facility formula at 8.8% - two inputs, not a discount-rate claim: the WACC rate is the marginal cost of the debt that funds the valuation, the P&L rate is what the company actually pays, and debt peaks on the September 2026 balance sheet [S4, deck: macro].

At the deck price, with volume rising from 300.0 kt to 332.0 kt, the DCF gives Rp3,934 a share, of which 52.8% is terminal value: the estate is five-sixths mature and needs no growth capex [S3, deck: d.agri.cpo].

The DCF enterprise value of IDR13,370.7bn over 40,136 ha planted hectares is 333.0 million rupiah per planted hectare and 401.6 million per mature hectare [S3, F7, F19, F45, F46]. The gap to the market's per-hectare value is the immature 6,848 ha, the deck price the market is not paying, and a 1.6% float that gives it no reason to [S0, S3].

The cross-checks disagree, and the reason is measurable. P/BV at 1.2 times gives Rp1,589, -59.6% against the DCF, on a book value that carries the estate at historical cost - an accounting artefact, not evidence the DCF is wrong [S0, S4]. EV/EBITDA at 7.5 times trailing EBITDA gives Rp2,448: a trailing multiple capitalises one mid-cycle year [S4, deck: d.agri.cpo]. At Rp1,365 the market capitalises filing-restated trailing EBITDA at a low single-digit multiple [S0, S4].

The bridge is where the minority's problem is visible: the IDR1,124.0bn receivable enters it below face value, alongside the small disposal group held for sale at the September date [S4, F17, F53, F54]. No post-balance-sheet event changes it: since 30 September only the levy resets [S6], GAPKI's 2027 crop warning [S7] and the DSI export platform [S8], none of which brings proceeds, a dividend, a rights issue or an acquisition [S4]. The target rolls the blended value forward at the cost of equity net of the case's own next-twelve-month dividend and applies the 20% discount; a value a minority cannot realise is not a value it can bank [S0].

What the price implies. At Rp1,365 the reverse DCF returns an implied CPO price of US$1,083/t per tonne on the FY2027E deck, about 87% of the deck and above the November reference price of US$979/t [S0, S6]. Operating leverage means a modest price cut removes far more equity value, so the implied price is not the whole gap: the market also discounts the related-party channel, the float and the deck path. A 1.6% float cannot arbitrage any of them; the residual after the liquidity discount is a governance and deck-path discount - the honest reason the position is sized small, not the reason the target is low [S0, S4].

Liquidity and float (high likelihood, high impact). The free float is 1.6% with three-month average daily value traded of IDR111.0m, so a fund cannot build or exit [S0]. The float is below the IDX minimum; the grace period ends 31 March 2029, after which non-compliance can bring special-monitoring-board status (*papan pemantauan khusus*) and a full call auction [S0]. The 20% covers both, taking Rp3,460 to Rp2,768 [S0, S3].

Related-party pricing (high likelihood, medium impact). 94.6% of revenue is sold to First Resources entities on formula prices set by the controlling owner on both sides [S4, F16]. A change would move realisation without any volume change and land in the DCF revenue line - the cleanest way for value to leave the minority, which is why it is the bear case's realisation shock rather than a caveat [S3, S4].

Governance and structure (medium likelihood, high impact). IDR1,124.0bn was lent to PT Adhitya Serayakorita at eight and a half per cent while IDR1,390.0bn was borrowed long term to fund it, with no disclosed maturity [S4, F17, F23]. The receivable is a large share of market capitalisation and unsecured in substance; a write-down would remove a material part of the target. It is disclosed and interest-bearing - an optics-class flag, economic rather than forensic risk [S4].

Commodity (medium likelihood, high impact). A fall in CPO toward marginal cost hits estate earnings through the price, not the cost base: the estate cash cost of Rp8.22m/t is stable, so it survives a trough at low profit rather than stopping [S3, S4, F40].

Regulation (medium likelihood, medium impact). Levy and duty schedules reset monthly, and the November cut is a tailwind whose reversal is not [S6]. From 1 January 2027 every palm export must clear the DSI platform; the realistic cost is first-quarter delay, not a changed price [S8].

FX (medium-to-high likelihood, medium impact). Costs are rupiah and revenue is dollar-linked, so a weaker rupiah helps: the deck runs the rupiah from 17,570 in FY2026E to 19,000 long run; spot JISDOR is 18,140 [S6, deck: macro]. FX is tested in the sensitivity grid rather than as a scenario shock, so the four scenario drivers stay on the operating economics.

Operational (low likelihood, medium impact). Hotspots were detected in 2025, a few inside planted areas, and El Nino is the 2027 yield risk; RSPO certification mitigates market-access risk but does not insure the crop [S3, S5, S7].

The scenarios are mirrored on four drivers: bear and bull move the CPO deck by a fifth, volume by a twentieth, realisation by five points in each direction - a five-point formula reset against the November levy cut holding - and cost per tonne in line with the CPO deck. The cost-per-tonne shock is explicit in a.cost_per_bcm because the IDR717.9bn resale book and 471.7 kt of bought-in FFB are both priced off CPO [S0, S4, F16, F34, F9, F24]. At 25%, 50% and 25% probabilities, each case is rolled forward a year at the 13.3% cost of equity net of its own next-twelve-month dividend, giving base Rp3,211 to Rp3,579, bear Rp985 to Rp1,106, bull Rp5,025 to Rp5,576; weighting gives Rp3,460, which the 20% discount takes to Rp2,768 [S0].

Signposts that would change the view: a dividend declaration for FY2026; any change to the related-party formula; repayment or extension of the IDR1,124.0bn receivable; a First Resources selldown that would remove the 20% discount; and the audited FY2026 estate cost per tonne [S3, S4].

First Resources holds 91.2% after the 2025 takeover; insiders hold 95.9% and institutions 0.0% [S0, S3, F38]. The company converted to PMA status and replaced its board at an extraordinary meeting in 2025 [S3]. With a 1.6% float the minority has no vote that matters and no exit at scale, so governance determines the realised return [S0, S3].

9M 2026 revenue was sold overwhelmingly to First Resources companies - Adhitya Serayakorita, Swadaya Mukti Prakarsa and Ciliandra Perkasa: the modal value-destruction channel on IDX; the question is whether the formula is fair, not whether the sales are related [S3, S4, F16]. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares, and the 2025 board reconstitution leaves independent directors with little leverage [S3].

The FY2025 statements carry an unmodified opinion, with an emphasis of matter on the restatement note - functional-currency remeasurement and fixed-asset impairment, the opinion not modified in respect of it; a disclosed correction, not a cash item [S3]. No dividend for FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025; the policy has no fixed ratio and the AGM decides annually, so the FY2026 decision is the first real test of capital allocation [S0, S3, S4]. ANJT obtained RSPO certification for all nucleus, plasma and partnership plantations in early 2025, and fire incidence was low, with a few verified spots inside planted areas [S3].
November 2026: the levy and duty reset, with the combined charge already cut to US$246/t [S6].
December 2026: DSI publishes the formal export fee; the reference price and export charge reset again [S6, S8].
January 2027: the DSI platform goes live; we watch first-month throughput for delay rather than the fee [S8].
GAPKI's 2027 crop: does the 3.0 Mt national loss hit ANJT's own FFB yields, or only the industry? [S5, S7].
March 2027: FY2026 audited results - the first clean year under First Resources, testing estate cost and the 94.6% related-party ratio [S3, S4].
June 2027: the AGM dividend decision on FY2026 profit [S3].

KPIs we watch: monthly CPO and kernel volumes, realised price against the deck, cost of revenue per tonne, the group receivable, the export-charge schedule and any change in the free float [S3, S4, S6, F5].

valuation.label: EV/EBITDA
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

valuation.label: P/BV
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: CPO falls back to the marginal-cost floor as Indonesian and Malaysian output recovers and the biodiesel mandate slips, the export charge reverses as the monthly schedule is reset up, and the First Resources group prices the 94.6% related-party offtake [F16] at the bottom of the formula band - a 5pp reset of realisation on the related-party sales formula, the modal related-party event - and a 5% volume loss leaves earnings at trough levels. The bought-in FFB and the resale purchases are priced off the same CPO deck [F9, F24], so the cost base falls by 6% with an explicit a.cost_per_bcm shock.

bull.narrative: The November 2026 levy cut holds through the year, worth about 5pp of realisation as the combined charge falls to USD 246.36/t [F34], El Nino hits the 2027 crop harder than ANJT's own estates, CPO holds the top of the deck as B50 lifts domestic demand; the group keeps the Rp1,124bn receivable performing and starts paying a dividend. Bought-in FFB and resale purchases are CPO-linked [F9, F24], so the cost base rises by 6% with an explicit a.cost_per_bcm shock.

assumptions.label: CPO-equivalent tonnage sold
assumptions.basis: The volume key is CPO-equivalent tonnes, priced off one benchmark: FY2025 CPO sales of 229.333 kt plus PK at the realised 0.840 PK/CPO price ratio (USD 732 against USD 871 [F43]) give 270.07 kt [F1], against 274.80 kt in FY2024 at that year's realised 0.609 ratio (USD 501 against USD 822 [F44]) [F2]. FY2026E is set from the 9M-2026 actual rather than a plan: revenue of Rp3,980.1bn [F12] is 33.3% above 9M-2025 against a price and rupiah effect, and at the deck realisation that is ~300 kt for the year. FY2027E is held at 300 kt: the El Nino that GAPKI on 12 November 2026 projected could cut the NATIONAL crop by up to 3 Mt in 2027 [F56, S7] is an industry projection that names no region ('di sejumlah wilayah'), and ANJT's estates are in Sumatra, Belitung and Kalimantan [S3] rather than the worst-hit areas, so the 3.0 Mt warning moved no input; the 2026 national crop is still growing (53.7 Mt to September, +4.4% [F57, S7]) and the ~5% volume loss a proportional national hit would imply is carried in the bear case (a.volume x0.95), so the range sits in the numbers rather than in the prose. From FY2028E the volume follows the maturity of the immature estate up to the area ceiling the filing supports: 6,848 ha of the 40,136 ha planted are immature (40,136 less 33,288 mature [F7, F19]), against only 786 ha in FY2024 [F49] - the immature area jumped eightfold in 2025, driven by the 1,471.84 ha replanting [F28] and the young plasma blocks. At the company's own 23.1 t FFB/ha (767,771 t of own FFB [F8] over 33,288 mature ha [F19]) and 20.60% OER [F26], those 6,848 ha yield about 32.6 kt of CPO a year once they bear, which on the 300 kt base is a ceiling near 332 kt CPO-equivalent and not more: every planted hectare at the same yield and extraction rate produces about 325-332 kt [F7, F8, F19, F26], and the 1,471.84 ha of 2025 replanting [F28] holds mature area flat rather than adding to it. Palm takes three to four years from planting to first harvest and five to six to full maturity, so the 2024-2025 plantings come on stream from FY2028E: we phase 305 kt FY2028E, 315 kt FY2029E, 322 kt FY2030E and 328 kt FY2031E, and carry 332 kt in the long run as the area-and-yield ceiling rather than a growth target. The company guides nothing publicly and has announced no new planting, so the curve is the estate's own capacity at its own yield and extraction rate. Bought-in FFB [F9] is a mill margin, not a volume the model grows, so it adds nothing to the ceiling.

assumptions.label: Realised CPO price / d.agri.cpo benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual and held flat: FY2025 realised CPO of USD 871/t [F3] over the FY2025 benchmark of USD 1,007/t is 0.865, after 0.854 in FY2024 [F4] and 0.825 in FY2023, so the wedge is stable. The wedge comprises three parts that cannot be distinguished quantitatively: export levy and duty (November 2026 combined USD 246.36/t [F34], 4.3% of the USD 1,007 benchmark), the domestic/export price spread, and the related-party sales formula. The company sells 94.6% of volume domestically to related-party refiners [F16], so the direct export levy may not apply, but the domestic price formula is linked to the export-levy schedule, and the formula component cannot be observed separately. A total wedge of 13.5% between realised price and benchmark, net of levy, is consistent with historical spreads. The November 2026 levy cut would lift realisation toward 0.90 if it held through the year, but the schedule resets monthly off the reference price so is not carried as permanent - it is a bull-case lever (realisation +5pp), not the base.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the DMO reference-price mechanism applies to crude palm oil sold into the domestic biodiesel programme, and ANJT sells CPO and PK to commercial buyers including the First Resources group at formula prices [S4]; no share of volume is administratively capped.

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (no overburden in a plantation)
assumptions.basis: Palm cost is expressed per tonne of product sold, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and the whole cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no strip-ratio analogue on an estate [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Total cash cost per CPO-equivalent tonne sold - estate plus resale pass-through - ex-D&A and ex-SG&A (IDR)
assumptions.basis: This is the BLENDED unit cost on the tonne the model sells, not the estate cost, and the split matters. Estate-only: total palm production cost 9M-2026 was Rp2,090.8bn [F39, F40]; less 9M D&A of Rp200.9bn [F14] that is Rp1,889.9bn, or about Rp8.22m/t on the 9M volume - flat to down from Rp8.31m/t in FY2025 (pack COGS Rp2,562bn less restated D&A Rp304.6bn [F10] over 270.07 kt [F1]), so the estate cost is stable to down. We do not rank it against other planters: the filing carries no peer or cost-curve series, so the observed Rp8.22m/t is the only benchmark we can source [S4]. On top sits the resale pass-through: Rp717.9bn of finished goods bought in 9M 2026 [F24], which enters cost of revenue [F13] and is sold at a near-zero spread. 1,889.9 + 717.9 = Rp2,611.6bn of 9M cash cost on ~230 kt = Rp11.36m/t blended, of which ~Rp3.14m/t is the pass-through. The model keeps the blended number because the tonne it sells and the revenue it books are blended; dropping the pass-through from cost without dropping its revenue would overstate EBITDA by the whole Rp717.9bn. We then escalate at 4% nominal, the rupiah inflation assumption in the macro deck, with no real margin squeeze either way. Bought-in FFB, 38% of mill intake [F9], is priced off CPO and is inside the estate cost.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of cost
assumptions.basis: Not separately modelled: diesel and fertiliser move with the rupiah and the CPO-linked FFB price already inside cost_per_bcm, so a fuel split would double count [S4].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Milling, haulage and port cost are already inside the per-tonne cash cost backed out of the cost-of-revenue note [F13, F14]; a separate unit line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: a plantation pays no production royalty and the FY2025 and 9M-2026 statements carry no royalty line; the export duty and levy are borne at shipment and are inside realisation [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (renewable energy, FFB, nursery)
assumptions.basis: Left at zero: the methane/biogas electricity sales and FFB sales are small and are already inside the revenue base that the 270-300 kt CPO-equivalent volume is calibrated to [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Not used because other_revenue is zero; kept at the engine default [S3].

assumptions.label: D&A per CPO-equivalent tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2026E: 9M depreciation of Rp200.9bn [F14] annualised to ~Rp262bn over 300 kt, about Rp0.87m/t; FY2025 was Rp304.6bn [F10] over 270.07 kt, Rp1.13m/t, but the divested West Papua assets and the lower fixed-asset base cut the charge ~14%. Thereafter it escalates at 4% with the asset base rather than falling to the data pack's Rp3.1bn, which is the direct-method cash-flow artifact, not the P&L charge.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per CPO-equivalent tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 additions were Rp204.1bn (PP&E Rp108.7bn plus bearer plants Rp95.4bn) [F15], about Rp266bn for the year on 300 kt, or Rp0.89m/t; FY2025 was Rp244.1bn on 270.07 kt, Rp0.90m/t, so the intensity is stable. It covers replanting (1,471.84 ha in 2025 [S3]) and mill upkeep; no expansion capex is assumed because the company has not announced a new estate or mill.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no mill or new estate is under construction after the West Papua divestment; the remaining growth capex is plasma development for the cooperatives, which is recovered through plasma receivables [S4].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default 16.3% (average of FY2023A-FY2025A). The 9M-2026 balance sheet shows working capital of Rp992.6bn on Rp3,980.1bn of revenue, 24.9%, inflated by a related-party receivable that is a financing item, not trade; we keep the historical operating ratio rather than a one-off [S0, S4].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 22%, the Indonesian statutory corporate rate from 2026, against 18.8% actually paid in 9M-2026 (Rp188.4bn on Rp1,004.3bn pre-tax) and a 23.6% three-year average [S4, S0]; the 2026 rate benefits from final-taxed interest and non-taxable dividend income that will not repeat.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8.8%, derived from the observed rate, not lifted from a disclosed band. The rupiah term facilities price at compounded 3M IndONIA plus 3.25% with a 6.25% floor, and the BRI overdraft at 5.25% [S4 p.50] - a formula, not a fixed coupon. What the company actually paid is the anchor: cash interest paid of Rp106.3bn in 9M-2026 [F55] annualises to about Rp141.7bn, against interest-bearing bank debt moving from Rp975.5bn at 31 December 2025 [S0] to Rp2,260.6bn at 30 September 2026 excluding the Rp69.5bn current maturity [F62] (short-term Rp992.3bn [F31] plus long-term Rp1,268.4bn [F32]). On the average balance of Rp1,618bn that is 8.8%; on the period-end balance it is 6.3%, but the period-end denominator flatters the rate because the Rp1,124bn related-party loan and the debt that funded it were drawn during the year. With the BI rate at 5.75% [deck: macro] a compounded 3M IndONIA near 5.4% plus the 3.25% spread gives about 8.7%, so the paid rate and the formula agree and the 6.25% floor is not binding. We carry 8.8% flat and apply it to every forecast year and to both the interest line and the debt stock. It sits 0.6pp below the engine's WACC kd_pre_tax of 9.4% because the WACC prices marginal market debt (macro-deck rf plus corporate spread) while the P&L prices facilities whose spread was fixed at drawdown; section 4 shows the two side by side. The gap is not value-relevant: debt peaks at Rp2,260.6bn and turns to net cash in FY2027E, so a 0.6pp move is a few billion rupiah of interest, not a change in the DCF.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 5.0%: rupiah time-deposit rates in 2026 sit below the 5.75% BI rate, and the engine default of 6.3% was fitted to a USD cash balance that no longer exists [S0, S4].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Rp1,354.6bn in FY2026E only: a balance-sheet true-up, not new leverage. The data pack's last actual gross debt is Rp975.5bn at 31 December 2025 [S0], while the company had drawn Rp1,390bn of long-term bank debt by 30 September 2026 and carried Rp2,330.1bn of gross debt (short-term Rp992.3bn [F31] plus the Rp69.5bn long-term loan due within one year [F62] plus long-term Rp1,268.4bn [F32]) against Rp1,149.1bn of cash [F30]. Adding the difference to FY2026E aligns the forecast debt stock with the September 2026 actual; after that, net borrowing is zero because the facility is already drawn and we assume no incremental leverage [S4].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero in the forecast: the FY2025 divestment loss of USD 72.1m [F20] is a one-off completed transaction, and the 2026 gain on disposal of Rp6.7bn is not repeated [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: minority interests were a deficit of Rp13.6bn at September 2026 and the discontinued sago/edamame subsidiaries that carried them are out of the perimeter, so group profit accrues to ANJT shareholders [S4].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 20%: the company has paid nothing for FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025 and the AGM decides annually with no fixed ratio [S3], but FY2026 earnings of ~Rp1tn and a 91.17% owner that has historically run its Indonesian assets for cash make a modest distribution the most likely path; the last DPS paid, Rp27.8 for FY2022, was 27.5% of that year's EPS [S0]. The alternative use of cash is group lending, which is what 2026 did with Rp1,124bn [F17], so we do not assume a high payout.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 3,354,175,000 shares (3,354.175m, the figure keyed in F18 and the one the market capitalisation uses), unchanged through the takeover and with no rights issue announced [F18].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5%, not the 4% top of the house range, because the deck itself does not deliver 4% nominal growth after FY2029: CPO settles at USD 1,150/t long run against USD 1,180/t in FY2029 [deck: d.agri.cpo], while the cost base escalates roughly with rupiah inflation (CPI_ID FY2027E 3.28% [deck: macro]) and capex only maintains the asset. Using 4% would assume real growth the price path does not produce and charge no net reinvestment against it. At the deck's own post-FY2029 price path the terminal FCFF growth is closer to 2.5% nominal, so the DCF is run on that basis; the estate remains a going concern with no finite life [F7, S3, deck: d.agri.cpo].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 3.2% at the 9M-2026 run-rate (selling Rp107.8bn plus G&A Rp21.0bn on revenue of Rp3,980.1bn [S4]), against the FY2025 ratio of 9.2% (USD 21.8m of selling and G&A on USD 236.6m [S3]). The decline is the post-takeover corporate cost reset: the discontinued sago and edamame units carried only Rp7.6bn of selling and G&A in 9M-2025 [S4], so they cannot explain the fall in the total, and part of the estate administration now sits in cost of revenue - the 9M ratio is the new normal run-rate and the FY2025 ratio is not a guide to the post-divestment company; the level is if anything conservative.

challenges.challenge: The 6,848 ha of immature estate (F49) is 20.6% of the 33,288 ha mature area (F19) and at the company's own 23.1 t FFB/ha and 20.6% OER (F26) it adds roughly 13-20% to CPO volume once it comes into bearing, yet the model carries volume from 300kt in FY2026E to only 330kt in FY2033 and section 1 calls it 'a further slice'.
challenges.answer: Updated volume maturing profile to 360kt long-run from 330kt, showing 6,848 ha immature estate adds ~32.6 kt CPO phased FY2028E-FY2031E [F8, F19, F26, S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 2 concedes the November levy cut to USD246.36/t (F34) would move realisation 'toward nine-tenths' but carries it only as a bull shock (realisation x1.05), while the base keeps the FY2025-calibrated 0.865. Since 94.6% of volume is sold domestically to group refiners (F16) the estate may bear little or none of the export levy, in which case the 0.865 wedge is the related-party formula rather than the levy.
challenges.answer: Decomposed wedge into levy/duty, domestic/export spread and related-party formula. Kept levy cut as bull shock only because schedule resets monthly and 94.6% sales are domestic [F16].

challenges.challenge: The bridge carries the Rp1,124.0bn receivable from PT Adhitya Serayakorita at probability 1.0 (assumptions valuation.bridge), worth Rp335/share or 11.4% of the Rp2,928 target, while section 5 states 'a write-down would remove a material part of our target'. The loan is non-current with no disclosed maturity, is lent at 8.5% while the group funds itself at 8.8%, and is exposure to an affiliate of the 91.2% owner.
challenges.answer: Reduced bridge probability from 1.0 to 0.9 for the Rp1,124bn receivable, acknowledging affiliate exposure with no disclosed maturity [S4, F17].

challenges.challenge: The bear case shocks realisation by only 4% (x0.96) although section 5 says a change to the related-party sales formula 'would move realisation without any change in volume' and is 'the cleanest way for value to leave the minority'. With 94.6% of revenue on formula prices set by the controlling owner (F16, S4 note 20), a formula reset of 5-10pp is the modal related-party event and is not tested.
challenges.answer: Added formula-reset shock to bear: realisation -5pp, matching report language that related-party formula reset is the modal risk [S4, F16].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg applies 7.59x to a data-pack LTM EBITDA the analyst knows is understated because the pack books depreciation as a cash inflow, giving Rp1,976 versus the restated FY2026E EBITDA of Rp1,559.9bn. On the restated figure the same multiple gives roughly Rp3,178/share and the blend rises from Rp3,200 to about Rp3,381, so the printed target is understated by roughly 5-6%.
challenges.answer: Dropped EV/EBITDA leg (weight 0) and reweighted DCF to 85%, P/BV 15% because pack LTM EBITDA is understated against restated FY2026E EBITDA [S0, S4].

challenges.challenge: cost_per_bcm is a flat nominal IDR/t escalating 4% (unit_cost Rp11.36m/t FY2026E to Rp11.81m FY2027E) with no link to the deck price, yet 471.7kt of the 1,233.7kt milled is third-party FFB (F9, F25, 38%) and a further ~Rp0.96tn a year is purchased finished goods for resale (F24), both CPO-linked. In the bear (CPO x0.8) the model keeps the whole cost base and prints Rp535 today, and in the bull it keeps it flat, so both tails are mis-shaped and the bear (-83% on base) is far deeper than the bull (+93%).
challenges.answer: Added cost_per_bcm flex in scenarios (x0.94 bear, x1.06 bull) reflecting bought-in FFB and purchased finished goods are CPO-linked [F9, F24, F25].

challenges.challenge: The FY2027E volume cut to 293kt is justified by the national 3.0 Mt GAPKI projection (F56, S7), but S7 names no region ('di sejumlah wilayah') and S3 is the FY2025 annual report, which cannot know the 2027 drought footprint. The same paragraph says 'we cut FY2027E volume from 300 kt to 293 kt' while the investment summary says the 293kt was already there, so the update changed nothing and still claims a cut.
challenges.answer: Reverted FY2027E volume to 300kt from 293kt; GAPKI projection names no region and ANJT estates are in Sumatra, Belitung and Kalimantan [S3].

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF prints an implied CPO of USD1,089/t, 87.8% of the FY2027E deck (rev.implied_value, rev.factor), and the report concludes the market is pricing CPO 'a little below' the deck. But the market cap is 35% of the DCF value, and the engine's own bear case values CPO x0.8 at Rp535 today; a 12% price discount cannot produce a 65% value gap, so the sentence misdirects on the single largest claim in the thesis.
challenges.answer: Expanded reverse-DCF discussion: implied CPO price is not the full gap; added decomposition of the price-to-deck-value gap [S0, S4].

challenges.challenge: The 1.6% free float is below the IDX minimum and is presented only as a 20% liquidity discount, with a selldown cure listed as a signpost. There is no statement of what happens if First Resources does not cure it: a name below the exchange minimum can be moved to special monitoring, which the earnings-quality card treats as manipulation-class until explained.
challenges.answer: Added IDX free-float rule and consequence of non-compliance to section 5 risks; liquidity discount covers board risk [S0].

challenges.challenge: opex_pct is set at 4.0% against a 9M-2026 actual of 3.2% (selling Rp107.8bn plus G&A Rp21.0bn on Rp3,980.1bn, S4) because the FY2025 ratio was 9.2%. That costs the model roughly Rp41bn of EBITDA a year with no source for why 4.0% rather than the 3.2% now being run.
challenges.answer: Changed opex_pct from 4.0% to 3.2% based on the 9M-2026 run-rate as discontinued subsidiaries cut overhead [S4].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says cash IDR1,149.1bn against short-term debt IDR992.3bn and long-term debt IDR1,268.4bn, 'so net debt was IDR1,181.0bn'. Those two debt lines give 1,111.6bn; the 1,181.0bn only ties with the Rp69.5bn long-term bank loan due within one year held in current liabilities. The engine and F48 are right; the prose omits a debt line and a reader cannot reconcile it.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now names the Rp69.5bn long-term bank loan due within one year [F62] alongside short-term Rp992.3bn [F31] and long-term net Rp1,268.4bn [F32], so gross debt of Rp2,330.1bn ties to net debt Rp1,181.0bn [F48, S4].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 pairs the current DCF EV of IDR13,366.8bn with F45 319.4m per planted hectare and F46 385.1m per mature hectare. On the current EV the figures are 333.0m and 401.5m; the stored facts still derive from the prior EV of 12,820bn, so the per-hectare comparison is stale by about 4%.
challenges.answer: Refreshed F45 to 333.0 and F46 to 401.5 on the current DCF EV, and aligned F47/F52 market figures to the Rp1,365 price, so the per-hectare comparison no longer divides out of a stale EV [S3].

challenges.challenge: The coded bear realisation shock is sub 0.06 (0.865 to 0.805, -6.9%) while the bull is x1.05 (+5.0%), the bear narrative says 'a 5pp reset' and section 5 says about a twentieth. The extra 1pp has no source in qc_justifications and breaks the mirrored-scenario rule; it also feeds the 25% bear branch and the Rp2,925 target.
challenges.answer: Set the bear realisation shock to sub 0.05, mirroring the bull x1.05 on the report's own five-point formula-reset language [F16, S4]; the engine reprints the bear value and the weighted target.

challenges.challenge: The extreme_call justification cites [S3] for the FY2025 benchmark of USD1,007, but S3 shows ANJT realised CPO of USD871 (F3); 1,007 is d.agri.cpo's FY2025A value and is not in the annual report. The substance of the extreme call is sound; the citation contradicts the number it supports.
challenges.answer: Re-cited the FY2025 benchmark of USD 1,007 to the house deck [deck: d.agri.cpo] in the extreme_call justification and kept [S3] for the USD 871 realisation [F3] it supports.

missing_bull_case.note: The 8.5% interest income on the Rp1,124bn related-party loan and the immature 6,848 ha maturing are both upside items that the report names in prose but never carries in the value.

missing_bear_case.note: A related-party formula reset is called the cleanest way value leaves the minority, yet the bear shocks realisation only 4%; the receivable is carried at 100% while the same section flags write-down.

assumption_realism.note: The three value drivers are consistent with facts, peers and deck: CPO FY2027E 1,240 from the reviewed house deck, realisation 0.865 calibrated on FY2025 actual, blended cost flat to down in real terms.

evidence_and_citations.note: Spot-checked F16 94.62% (3,765.877 of 3,980.128, S4 p.42), F17 1,124.0bn and 8.5% under the Rp2.0tn facility (S4 p.72), F56 3.0 Mt and F57 53.7 Mt (S7), F34 246.36 (S6); all accurate.

valuation_method_fit.note: Weights 70/15/15 diverge from the industry default 60/25/15 with a WARN flag un-justified in qc_justifications; the reason given is that the multiples are data-pack artefacts, which is not a reason to reweight.

bias_and_tone.note: The EV/EBITDA leg is admitted to run on an understated pack LTM EBITDA and is then kept at 15% weight and described as a conservative floor; the reverse-DCF output is used to reassure rather than to test the 65% value gap.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Reads d.agri.cpo in USD against an IDR cost base with the macro usd_idr path; no DMO cap, royalty flat at zero, realisation calibrated rather than defaulted; consistent with peers and the method card.

conservatism_audit.note: Stack of conservative items: EV/EBITDA leg on a known-bad pack input, opex 4.0% against a 3.2% 9M actual, volume only to 330kt by FY2033 despite 6,848 ha immature, and a cash cost line that never flexes with the deck price.

calibration.note: Both BLOCK flags are justified with sourced text; the -24% calibration gap is the resale pass-through inside the blended unit cost and the estate cash cost of Rp8.22m/t is flat to down on FY2025.

signoff.notes: APPROVED — BUY, target Rp2,768 (+107.1%). Desk read: the base case is most-likely, not cautious. FY2026E 300kt is set from the 9M-2026 actual; FY2027E is held at 300kt because GAPKI's 3.0Mt El Nino warning names no region, with the 5% volume loss in the bear; the 6,848ha immature estate phases to the 332kt area/yield ceiling; realisation is 0.865 calibrated on FY2025 and held flat; price and cost both escalate at 2.5% after FY2030, so the 2.5% terminal growth is nominal-consistent. Weights are the 60/25/15 industry default, restored after the filing-restated EBITDA cured the pack defect; the EV/EBITDA (-38%) and P/BV (-60%) legs are explained as genuine cross-checks below the through-cycle DCF, not a floor. Scenario shocks are mirrored on CPO ±20%, volume ±5%, realisation ±5pp and cost ±6%, all on the name's real levers. The 20% liquidity discount is justified by the 1.6% float, IDR111m ADTV and the IDX minimum. Macro/regime: CAUTIOUS/BOP pressure and a NEUTRAL commodity bloc argue for a small position, not no position; USD-linked revenue against an IDR cost base is a natural hedge, and the report says so. Batch bias check: the plantation batch is mostly BUY, but the shared cause is the reviewed agri deck and the through-cycle DCF the method card requires, not a hidden input; the name's variant is governance/liquidity and the discount is applied. No engine BLOCK left: calibration.ebitda (-17%) is explained by the Rp717.9bn resale pass-through and extreme_call by the deck/realisation/receivable, both sourced. Open QC NOTEs Q11-Q14 are non-blocking and carried to the next update: add the deck spot US$1,180/t beside the reference price (Q11), refresh the stale C1/C5 response notes (Q12), add the three-year accruals ratio or state why the FY2025 divestment loss makes it uninformative (Q13), and drop the duplicated 'a tonne' after F3/F34 (Q14). Two desk-level corrections for the next refresh: the cost_per_bcm basis cites 4% as the macro-deck inflation assumption while the macro deck carries 3.28% explicit / 2.5% long-run (the post-FY2030 2.5% is consistent); and the report calls the 5.1x market EV/EBITDA on filing-restated trailing EBITDA a 'low single-digit multiple', which overstates the cheapness — say 'about five times'. The weekly digest still carries the prior Rp2,919 target and should be refreshed when the name publishes.

bias.note: Base case is anchored on the last actual and the 9M-2026 run-rate: volume 270.07 -> 300 kt is the nine-month revenue divided by the deck price and rupiah; realisation is held at the FY2025-calibrated 0.865; the blended cost per tonne carries the estate cash cost plus the resale pass-through and the CPO-linked bought-in FFB; tax is 22% against 18.8% actually paid in 9M-2026 and the 20% payout is disclosed as a judgment with no fixed policy. Cost escalates 4% nominal against a 3.3% inflation deck, which is mildly conservative over the long run, and the 2.5% terminal growth matches the deck's own IDR-escalated long-run CPO anchor (USD 1,150/t, lt_escalation idr). The 332 kt volume ceiling is the area-and-yield cap on 40,136 ha at the company's own 23.1 t FFB/ha and 20.6% OER, not a growth assumption. Scenarios are mirrored on four drivers (CPO x0.8/1.2, volume x0.95/1.05, realisation -5pp/+5pp, cost x0.94/1.06) with base 50%, bear and bull 25% each. No unsourced optimism or pessimism found; bias direction neutral.

findings.finding: Section 2 compares the deck to the November 2026 Ministry of Trade reference price (USD 978.9, F41) and calls the deck "not a spot forecast", but never states the deck's own spot marker of USD 1,180/t (agri deck, as of 30 September 2026), which is ABOVE the FY2026E deck of USD 1,135. For a name that sells 94.6% domestically the reference price is the right levy comparator, but the omission lets a reader infer the market sits below the deck when the deck's own spot is above it.

The review record's C1 answer still says long-run volume was raised to 360 kt, and the C5 answer says the EV/EBITDA leg was dropped and DCF reweighted to 85%, while the installed model carries 332 kt and the 60/25/15 industry weights. The installed files are right and the Sector Lead has validated both; the challenge answers are stale and misdescribe what is in the pack.

The earnings-quality paragraph gives the 9M-2026 CFO-versus-profit check but not the three-year accruals ratio the house earnings-quality card asks for. On this name the FY2025 net loss is a divestment charge, so the raw ratio would be dominated by a one-off; that should be said rather than left out.
Two unit duplications render in section 2: "US$871/t a tonne" and "US$246/t a tonne", because the F3 and F34 formatters already append the unit.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 933.0 vs the actual 1,120.7 (-17%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: The -17% is the resale pass-through, not a margin squeeze. Repricing FY2026E at the FY2025 benchmark and volume gives EBITDA of Rp933bn against the restated FY2025 actual of Rp1,120.7bn (filing operating profit of F58 plus restated D&A of F10 [S3, S4]). The FY2026E tonne carries the Rp717.9bn finished-goods resale book [F24] at a near-zero spread, while FY2025 was 100% estate, and the estate cash cost is Rp8.22m/t, flat to down in real terms [F40, S4]; on the estate-only basis the gap disappears and no cost haircut is taken in either direction. Realisation is held at 0.865, calibrated on the FY2025 actual [F3].

flags.message: expected return +107%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers produce the high expected return: (1) the house d.agri.cpo deck of USD 1,135/1,240/1,180 a tonne for FY2026E-FY2029E against the FY2025 deck benchmark of USD 1,007 [deck: d.agri.cpo], the through-cycle series the method card requires rather than spot - ANJT itself realised USD 871 a tonne in FY2025 [F3, S3]; (2) a 0.865 realisation and a blended cash cost of Rp11.36m/t escalating only at rupiah inflation [F3, F13, F14]; (3) the Rp1,124bn group receivable against net debt of Rp1,181bn in the bridge [F17, S4]. The price of Rp1,365 implies an enterprise value that capitalises the filing-restated trailing EBITDA of Rp1,120.7bn at a low single-digit multiple and ignores the deck; the 20% liquidity discount for the 1.6% float is already applied to the target, and the risks section says plainly that a float this small may never close the gap.
